summary: Redwood team demoed ephemeral request preview and redaction controls across Console and API. Focus on toggles for request storage, live preview of redactions, ML and regex hybrid PII detection, KMS/HSM integration, and POC next steps. Customer asked about residency, audit logs, and fallback behavior. Agreed to pilot with anonymized logs and follow-up on pricing + on-prem checklist.
topics: Redaction policy testing and live preview
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Park: Alright everyone, thanks for joining, we can get started. I'm Ethan from Redwood, with Nadia our solutions engineer. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Hi hi this is Aisha — Head of AI at SummitCare.
[00:12] Luis Ortega: Luis here, security architect.
[00:14] Maya Patel: Maya, DevOps.
[00:16] Ethan Park: Great. Today's demo is focused on the ephemeral request preview and redaction controls across the Console and the API. We'll show how you can toggle request storage, run a live redaction preview, and configure hybrid PII detectors.
[00:30] Nadia Gomez: Quick note, we'll also touch on how Redwood Opti-... Redwood Optimize will suggest batching + quant profiles but only briefly, main thing is data handling.
[00:38] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Sounds good. Our main goals: no PII persisted by default, show auditors how redaction works, and verify latency impact when we enable redaction.
[00:48] Ethan Park: Perfect — we built the preview exactly for that. I'll share my screen and start in the Console. Give me one sec.
[00:58] [screen share starts]
[01:02] Ethan Park: Ok so this is the request storage page under Settings > Request Handling. Top-level toggle here is "Store requests" — by default you can set it to Off, Ephemeral, or Persistent. Ephemeral means the request payload is kept in memory long enough to write logs and run redaction, then it is wiped; Persistent writes to object storage with retention policy.
[01:24] Luis Ortega: When you say wiped, is that a logical delete or is it zeroed from disk? Our compliance team asks about remnant data.
[01:33] Nadia Gomez: Good question. It's zeroed on the application side and the object is removed; for Dedicated/Private we support customer-managed KMS + lifecycle that triggers secure deletion. There's a note in the security doc about shred policies.
[01:47] Maya Patel: If we run Private on-prem, we control the storage backend — so that helps. How about audit logs, we need an immutable trail.
[01:56] Ethan Park: Yes — audit logs are separate and kept for admin actions; request payloads are separate from audit logs. You can configure audit retention independently, and logs show redaction status and rule hits but do not contain raw PII when redaction is enabled.
[02:12] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Can you demo the live redaction preview? That's the feature we really wanted to see.
[02:18] Nadia Gomez: Absolutely. We're going to use an example chat request with a simulated patient record. I'll paste in a snippet. Note: transcription may sometimes show "K-V cache" or similar in backend names, sorry if that pops up.
[02:32] [Nadia pastes sample request]
[02:36] Nadia Gomez: The preview pane shows the original request on the left and a preview processor on the right. See here — the redaction engine highlights detected PII: names, social security-like tokens, and dates.
[02:48] Dr. Aisha Rahman: I see. It marked 'John Patient' and '555-22-3333' as SSN. How configurable are the rules?
[02:57] Nadia Gomez: You can apply a hybrid approach — default ML detector plus customer-defined regex. Rules are applied in order: regex rules first if you pin them, then ML for fuzzy detections. There's an option to create a suppression list for known tokens.
[03:10] Luis Ortega: Does regex run locally or on Redwood servers? Any latencies to be aware of?
[03:15] Ethan Park: Regex is evaluated within the same processing pipeline. For Hosted, it runs in our runtime; for Private/Dedicated you can configure them to execute in your VPC. Latency impact is usually sub-10ms per request for typical regex sets; big rule sets can increase it — Optimize will notify you.
[03:33] Maya Patel: If we want to redact only certain fields, say remove patient name but keep the encounter text, can we scope rules to JSON paths?
[03:41] Nadia Gomez: Yes — field-scoped rules by JSON path or protobuf fields. We also have a "surgical redact" mode that keeps context tokens but masks identified spans. In preview you can toggle between full-mask, token-replace, or keep-context modes.
[03:56] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Can you walk through a failure mode — what if the ML misses something?
[04:02] Nadia Gomez: Sure. There's an audit column called 'rule hits' and confidence thresholds. If ML confidence is low, preview will show it in yellow, and you can add a regex to catch that pattern. Also we support post-processing alerts: if any low-confidence hits occur, the request can be sent to a queued review workflow.
[04:18] Luis Ortega: And those queued items — are they stored with raw data? Because reviewers will need context.
[04:24] Ethan Park: For review flows, you can run them in ephemeral mode where reviewers see a redacted version with a one-time decryption token. Nothing is written to persistent storage unless you opt-in and set a retention policy.
[04:36] Dr. Aisha Rahman: That one-time decryption token — is that logged in audit?
[04:39] Nadia Gomez: Yes, audit logs record who requested the token and when; the token itself isn't stored.
[04:44] [05:00] Ethan Park: Next I'm going to switch to the API so you can see how toggles work programmatically. The endpoint is POST /v1/requests with header x-redwood-storage: ephemeral|persistent|none. If you send ephemeral, the runtime processes the request and returns a request_id but we don't persist the payload beyond the ephemeral window.
[05:22] Maya Patel: If we forget the header, is there a default?
[05:25] Ethan Park: Defaults come from the organization-level setting. You can also enforce per-route SLOs and storage policies via route policies.
[05:34] Dr. Aisha Rahman: About encryption — KMS integration for Private: do you support HSM-backed keys?
[05:40] Nadia Gomez: Yes, HSM-backed KMS is supported. For Private we can integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, or your on-prem HSM via standard KMIP. Keys are used for at-rest encryption of persistent request storage; ephemeral mode keeps encryption keys in memory and rotates them frequently.
[05:58] Luis Ortega: Is there a way to force tokenization instead of redaction, like replace PII with synthetic tokens to preserve referential integrity?
[06:06] Ethan Park: We have a tokenization mode which emits stable pseudonyms per key; you can configure a look-up map or deterministic tokenization with a salt. That's useful for analytics where you want to track the same user without exposing identity.
[06:20] [06:30] Nadia Gomez: I'm going to run a quick demo of the Rules editor — it's here under Security > Redaction rules. You can add a regex rule, set scope, choose "block persist" or "allow but redact" and preview against sample payloads. I'll add a regex for a custom insurance ID pattern.
[06:48] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Will that regex be applied retroactively in logs? We have months of historical logs for model performance evaluation.
[06:55] Nadia Gomez: Retroactive application depends — for stored payloads we have a backfill job that can reprocess historical data through current rule sets, but that's a batch job that we run with customer approval. It can be CPU intensive and we bill for processing time.
[07:10] Luis Ortega: Billing question — how are redaction and storage billed? Is it per token, per request, or flat for dedicated?
[07:17] Ethan Park: For Hosted, you pay per inference (token-based) plus a small per-request storage fee if persistent. Redaction compute is included in the inference price for up to X rules; large rule sets or batch backfills are additional. For Dedicated/Private we include compute in reserved capacity, so it's more about the capacity contract. We'll follow up with pricing examples.
[07:36] [07:45] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Let's try a scenario — we want ephemeral by default, but for flagged research requests we persist results for 30 days. How would that be set up?
[07:56] Nadia Gomez: You'd set org default = ephemeral. Then create a route policy for routes matching /research/* with x-redwood-storage persistent and a 30-day retention. You can also add a rule that only certain roles (e.g., data-science) can access persisted blobs.
[08:12] Maya Patel: Can retention be set by tag? We use tags heavily.
[08:16] Nadia Gomez: Yes, you can tag requests at ingestion and retention rules can be tag-based. In the Console we show retention mapping so it's auditable.
[08:26] [08:40] Ethan Park: Now switching to the live preview again — I'm toggling a few settings: ML confidence threshold to 0.85, enabling deterministic tokenization for names, and adding an allowlist for internal test IDs. You should see the preview update.
[08:55] Dr. Aisha Rahman: It's updating in real time, I like the side-by-side. The masked tokens preserve sentence flow — that's important.
[09:03] Luis Ortega: A quick question on the 'allowlist' — if someone mistakenly adds a production SSN to allowlist, is there a veto?
[09:10] Nadia Gomez: Allowlists are gated behind RBAC, and large changes trigger an approval workflow. Also, audit logs show who edited allowlists.
[09:19] Dr. Aisha Rahman: What about exporting logs for our internal analytics? We want to export redacted requests and keep meta fields.
[09:26] Ethan Park: We have export tools: you can export redacted payloads to your S3 or GCS with a configured schema. Exports strip raw PII unless you've allowed persistence. You can also stream to Kafka for downstream analytics.
[09:40] [09:55] Maya Patel: In the private deployment spec, is there a minimum hardware footprint to run redaction and preview without noticeable latency?
[10:02] Nadia Gomez: For our recommended private bundle we suggest 2-4 GPUs depending on expected RPS. Redaction is CPU-light but the inference runtime drives latency. We can provide benchmark numbers from similar customers.
[10:20] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Can Redwood run a smoke benchmark with our sample logs? We want a real measure of latency impact.
[10:25] Ethan Park: Yes — that's part of the POC. If you upload 1000 sample requests to the sandbox, we can run a bench with redaction rules turned on and share the latency distribution and cost delta.
[10:38] Luis Ortega: About compliance — do you support export controls or data residency to keep data in EU region?
[10:45] Nadia Gomez: Absolutely. Hosting region is configurable; for Hosted we have EU and US regions. For Dedicated you can pin to a region and for Private it's entirely in your control. Audit logs include region metadata.
[10:57] [11:10] Dr. Aisha Rahman: What happens if a redaction rule changes after persistence? For example, we tighten rules and want to retroactively redact stored payloads.
[11:18] Ethan Park: We support a backfill process: re-run persisted payloads through the new rule set and overwrite with redacted versions, optionally creating a retention checkpoint for compliance. We log the backfill job and its result.
[11:32] Maya Patel: Do you have an API for the backfill so we can call it ourselves?
[11:36] Nadia Gomez: Yes, there's a Backfill API and a Console job UI. For big datasets we typically coordinate a maintenance window.
[11:44] [12:00] Ethan Park: Quick detour — security controls: SSO/SAML, RBAC roles, and admin scopes are in the Admin > Access page. You can create a role that only allows review access to redaction queues without view raw payload permissions.
[12:15] Luis Ortega: Can you demonstrate the review queue UX?
[12:19] Nadia Gomez: Sure — switching to the Review Queue tab. Here a reviewer sees a redacted snippet and flags low-confidence spans. They can annotate and escalate. The one-time decryption token flow is shown here: you click 'Request Decrypt' it opens a modal that requires MFA and records the approval in audit.
[12:40] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Good. Also want to confirm: do you store model prompts and system messages?
[12:47] Ethan Park: By default prompts are treated like request payloads controlled by the same storage toggles. You can mark certain fields as 'always redact' at the route level.
[12:57] [13:15] Maya Patel: If we're doing deterministic tokenization for a name, is the token reversible? We need a reversible mapping for certain clinical workflows.
[13:23] Nadia Gomez: Reversible tokenization is available but only with HSM-protected key access and strict RBAC. It's documented under 'Tokenization and key policy'.
[13:35] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We have a long list of odd identifiers from partner systems. Is there an import tool for custom patterns?
[13:42] Nadia Gomez: Yes, you can bulk upload regexes or patterns as a CSV and tag them. We also provide a small console analyzer that suggests regexes based on sample logs.
[13:56] Luis Ortega: Anything about model traceability? We need to know which model version generated an output if there is a later audit.
[14:03] Ethan Park: We persist model metadata per request (model id, version, quant profile). Even in ephemeral mode we emit metadata to the trace logs; the raw prompt isn't persisted unless saved.
[14:16] [14:30] Dr. Aisha Rahman: A couple more quick checks — SLA for Dedicated: latency SLOs and penalties?
[14:38] Ethan Park: Dedicated comes with SLOs defined in the contract. Typical SLO is 99.9% availability for serving and 95th percentile latency targets; specific numbers depend on the capacity tier. We'll include sample SLOs in the follow-up.
[14:54] Maya Patel: For the POC, can we try both Hosted ephemeral and Private on-prem to compare?
[15:00] Nadia Gomez: Yes — common approach is run a two-arm POC: Hosted sandbox for quick verification and a Private smoke on a small infra footprint for latency/residency testing.
[15:14] Luis Ortega: About shared artifacts — can we get the security deck and a wiring diagram for Private?
[15:19] Ethan Park: We'll send the security deck and a wiring diagram. Also the on-prem runbook.
[15:26] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Great. One more question — in the rare case of system fallback when a detector crashes, do you have a safe default?
[15:34] Nadia Gomez: Yes, safe default is 'block persist' with alerting. If redaction pipeline fails, you can configure the policy to either block writes or to route the request to synchronous review. We don't default to persisting unredacted data.
[15:49] [16:00] Ethan Park: We're about halfway through — anyone want to pause and dive deeper on any section?
[16:05] Luis Ortega: Can we see a sample API call with headers and response?
[16:08] Ethan Park: Yeah, sending a sample curl now in chat — POST /v1/requests with x-redwood-storage: ephemeral and header x-redwood-redaction: on. Response includes request_id and redaction_summary.
[16:20] Dr. Aisha Rahman: When you say redaction_summary, what fields are in that?
[16:24] Nadia Gomez: It includes counts per PII type, rule_hits, and masked_tokens_ratio. It's safe to store in analytics.
[16:32] Maya Patel: Does redaction_summary include any examples of masked text for QA?
[16:36] Ethan Park: It includes sample spans but redacted; you can configure to include a hash reference to the raw span for deterministic tokenization retrieval.
[16:48] [17:00] Nadia Gomez: I'm going to simulate an edge case: a nested JSON payload where names are embedded in free text. The ML highlights a low-confidence span — you can click 'suggest regex' and the UI suggests a candidate. You can accept and apply it immediately to the rule set and re-run preview.
[17:20] Dr. Aisha Rahman: That would save a lot of manual work.
[17:23] Luis Ortega: How often do you recommend running backfills? We worry about costs.
[17:28] Ethan Park: Usually we run backfills only when a compliance rule changes or after a major regex deployment. For continuous detection improvements, we recommend incremental processing or sampling to control cost.
[17:40] [18:00] Maya Patel: Do you have a preview of the CLI for infra automation?
[18:05] Nadia Gomez: Yes, we have a CLI and Terraform modules. CLI can toggle organization defaults, create rules, and trigger backfills.
[18:14] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Could you outline the POC deliverables?
[18:19] Ethan Park: Deliverables: 1) Hosted sandbox run with your sample logs and redaction config, produce latency & cost report. 2) Optional Private smoke with small infra and wiring diagram. 3) Security artifacts and on-prem runbook. 4) Pilot pricing and contract draft.
[18:34] Luis Ortega: Timeline? We want to present to legal and infra in two weeks.
[18:38] Nadia Gomez: We can send pricing and docs by 9/14 and schedule the first sandbox run the week of 9/20. That fits.
[18:47] [19:00] Dr. Aisha Rahman: A quick question on multi-tenant: we run multiple product lines in the same account; can redaction rules be tenant-scoped?
[19:09] Ethan Park: Yes — rules can be scoped to routes, tenants, or org units. Policies cascade and you can set deny/allow overrides.
[19:20] Maya Patel: If we need custom compliance logging (export full audit dump monthly), can that be automated?
[19:26] Nadia Gomez: Yes, scheduled exports to your storage endpoint are supported. We can set a retention window per export.
[19:36] [19:50] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Anything on the roadmap we should be aware of?
[19:54] Ethan Park: Roadmap items: enhanced de-identification for free text, richer audit visualizations, and expanded region coverage. We also plan improved autosuggestions for regex rules using ML.
[20:07] Luis Ortega: Any competitor gaps you've observed?
[20:10] Nadia Gomez: Some competitors key off only regex or only ML; our hybrid and UI-driven preview tends to reduce manual tuning. Also our route-level storage toggles and tokenization features are differentiators.
[20:24] [20:45] Ethan Park: Wrapping up demo portion — before we go to Q&A, short recap of the steps we agreed: we'll run a sandbox with your logs, send pricing, and schedule the on-prem deep-dive.
[20:59] Dr. Aisha Rahman: I think that's everything for now. A few follow-ups: Can you include the sample wiring diagram and the list of supported KMS integrations?
[21:08] Ethan Park: Yes, we'll include those. Anything else?
[21:12] Maya Patel: Please include example retention policies and sample SLA numbers.
[21:16] Ethan Park: Noted.
[21:18] [21:30] Luis Ortega: On audit logs — can we get a CSV sample?
[21:34] Nadia Gomez: We'll attach a sample audit export.
[21:38] [21:45] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Perfect. Thank you both.
[21:50] Ethan Park: Thanks everyone. We'll send notes and action items.
[21:55] [Meeting end recap shared in chat]
[22:00] Ethan Park (closing): Quick final note — safe default is never to persist unredacted PII. If you decide to persist anything, ensure policy + key controls are in place.
[22:10] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Good, that helps our legal stance.
[22:15] [Transcript ends — recording stopped]
